title: Scientists of Modern India
summary: Srinivasa Aiyangar Ramanujan, FRS, one of India's greatest mathematical geniuses, was born at Erode, Tamil Nadu, on 22 December 1887; his family shifted to Kumbakonam. At school he was an able all-rounder but numbers drew him; at 13 he found G.S. Carr's Synopsis of Elementary Results in Pure Mathematics, which introduced him to mathematics. He kept notebooks (the three 'Ramanujan's Notebooks'), could not complete college, posed and solved problems in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society and in 1911 published a brilliant paper on Bernoulli numbers. He worked as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust, found G.H. Hardy's Orders of Infinity and wrote to him with 120 theorems and formulae; Hardy arranged his passage to London. He joined Trinity College and got a B.Sc. in less than two years, formed a team with Hardy and J.E. Littlewood, published many papers, was the second Indian elected Fellow of the Royal Society and the first Indian Fellow of Trinity College. He fell ill in 1917, returned to India in 1919 and died in 1920 aged 32.

Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman, born 7 November 1888 at Tiruchirapalli, Tamil Nadu, to a father who was a professor of physics and mathematics, grew up with Sanskrit, music and science. He topped the Indian Audit and Accounts Service exam and became Assistant Accountant General in Calcutta at 19 but gave up the post to join the Science College of Calcutta University as professor of physics. His love of music led him to study the veena, violin, tabla and mridangam; in 1921 he read a paper on the theory of stringed instruments before the Royal Society; in 1924 he became a Fellow of the Royal Society. On a voyage to England he was curious about the blue colour of the sea and found it was due to the scattering of sunlight by water molecules, writing a paper on molecular scattering of light. Raman Effect: when a monochromatic beam passes through a transparent substance it scatters; the broken light has two spectral lines of very low intensity (Raman lines) parallel to the incident line, showing that it is not monochromatic; it proved that light consists of particles called photons. He won the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1930, the first Asian to do so. He used his 'great mind as his laboratory' and inspired students.

Jagdish Chandra Bose was born on 30 November 1858 at Mymensingh (now Bangladesh), studied at St Xavier's College, Calcutta, and in 1885 became Assistant Professor of Physics at Presidency College, refusing salary because it was half of an Englishman's. He decided to recover the fame India enjoyed in ancient times. He made apparatus to study electric waves and, for his paper 'The Electromagnetic Radiation and Polarization of Electric Ray', was knighted in 1917 and became a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1920, the first Indian scientist in physics to receive this honour. He invented the Crescograph, which records even a millionth part of a millimetre of plant growth and movement; it showed that plants have a circulatory system and that the upward movement of sap is the activity of living cells; his other instruments showed that metals react to stimuli and get tired and recover after rest; his wireless inventions antedated Marconi's (first wireless coherer, a radio-signal detector).

Born 30 October 1909 in a Parsi family, Bhabha took a mechanical engineering degree at Cambridge and a doctorate in 1935 and worked on cosmic radiation until 1939. He joined the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, at Raman's request, wrote to Sir Dorabji Tata, and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) was started in 1945 in his ancestral home. India's first atomic research centre (now BARC) was set up at Trombay and the first atomic reactor, Apsara, under his guidance. He was the first chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission (1948), chaired the UN conference on the peaceful uses of atomic energy, received the Padma Bhushan and died in a plane crash in 1966. He is called the father of Indian nuclear science.

Vikram Ambalal Sarabhai studied cosmic rays under C.V. Raman and took his Ph.D. at Cambridge; cosmic rays are a stream of energy particles from outer space. He was the main personality behind India's first satellite Aryabhata, an industrialist (Sarabhai Chemicals, Glass, Geigy, Merck) who saved crores of rupees by manufacturing military hardware, antibiotics and penicillin in India, founded the Ahmedabad Textile Industry's Research Association and the Indian Institutes of Management, chaired INCOSPAR and the Atomic Energy Commission, set up the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS) and planned education through satellite. He got the Padma Bhushan (1966) and the Padma Vibhushan after death.

Dr Kalam, the 11th President of India, was born on 15 October 1931 at Rameshwaram, Tamil Nadu; he studied at Schwartz High School, Ramanathapuram, and took a degree in aeronautical engineering from the Madras Institute of Technology. At ISRO (1963–82) at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre he developed the SLV-3 which placed the Rohini satellite in orbit. As Director of DRDO from 1982 he led the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme with five projects – Prithvi, Trishul, Akash, Nag and Agni (surface-to-surface, which made India a member of the club of highly developed countries). The light carbon material designed for Agni was used to make calipers for polio-affected people, reducing their weight from 4 kg to 400 g, and to make stents for balloon angioplasty. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1997, integrated science with religion and philosophy and believed in relying on inner signals and doing duty selflessly.

sa: Describe any three contributions of Srinivasa Ramanujan.

He published a research paper on Bernoulli numbers (1911) and solved problems in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society; with G.H. Hardy and J.E. Littlewood he made amazing contributions in Cambridge and published many papers; he left the three notebooks of results and became FRS and the first Indian Fellow of Trinity College.
Describe the achievements of J.C. Bose.

He studied electric waves and was knighted (1917) and became FRS (1920); he invented the Crescograph recording plant growth; his instruments showed that metals respond to stimuli and tire; and he invented the first wireless coherer before Marconi.

When a single-coloured (monochromatic) beam passes through a transparent substance, it scatters; Raman found two weak spectral lines parallel to the incident light, so the scattered light was not monochromatic. The phenomenon is the Raman Effect and the lines are Raman lines; it proved that light is made of photons. He won the Nobel Prize in 1930.
Write about the contribution of Dr Homi Bhabha.

Bhabha led India into the atomic age: he got TIFR founded at his ancestral home in 1945, started BARC at Trombay and the reactor Apsara, chaired the Atomic Energy Commission (1948) and the UN conference on peaceful uses of atomic energy, and won the Padma Bhushan.
Describe the contributions of Vikram Sarabhai.

He studied cosmic rays under Raman, led the Aryabhata satellite project, founded industries and IIMs, chaired INCOSPAR and the Atomic Energy Commission, set up TERLS and planned satellite education for villages; he saved crores by producing antibiotics and military hardware in India.
la: Examine the early life, education and first employment of Sir J.C. Bose.

Jagdish Chandra Bose was born on 30 November 1858 at Mymensingh (now in Bangladesh), where he had his early education, and studied at St Xavier's College, Calcutta. In 1885 he became Assistant Professor of Physics at Presidency College, but refused his salary because it was nearly half of an Englishman's. He decided to become a scientist to recover the fame India enjoyed in ancient times. He built apparatus to study electric waves.

or: Examine the inventions and achievements of Sir J.C. Bose as a scientist.

He invented the Crescograph, which records a millionth part of a millimetre of plant growth and showed plants have a circulatory system; his instruments showed that even metals react to stimuli and get tired; he invented the wireless coherer before Marconi; he was knighted in 1917 and became FRS in 1920.

la: How did Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam cover a long journey from beginning to the post of President of India?

Born at Rameshwaram in 1931, he studied at Schwartz High School and the Madras Institute of Technology (aeronautical engineering). At ISRO (1963–82) he developed the SLV-3 that put Rohini in orbit. As Director of DRDO he led the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (Prithvi, Trishul, Akash, Nag, Agni) and made India self-reliant. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1997 and became the eleventh President of India.

or: Examine the role of Dr Kalam in making India strong in defence and space sectors.

He developed SLV-3 at ISRO and launched Rohini; at DRDO he developed Prithvi, Trishul, Akash, Nag and Agni, making India self-dependent; his light carbon material also helped polio patients and heart patients.

la: Describe the contributions of Srinivasa Ramanujan in the field of mathematics.

Ramanujan, born at Erode in 1887, showed unusual love of numbers; at 13 he read Carr's Synopsis. He wrote results in notebooks and solved problems in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society; in 1911 he published a paper on Bernoulli numbers. A clerk at the Madras Port Trust, he wrote to G.H. Hardy giving 120 theorems; Hardy took him to Trinity College, Cambridge, where he formed a team with Hardy and Littlewood, published many papers, became FRS and the first Indian Fellow of Trinity College. He died in 1920.
Describe the life and achievements of C.V. Raman.

Raman (born 1888, Tiruchirapalli) topped the IAAS exam and became Assistant Accountant General at 19 but left for physics at Calcutta University. He studied musical instruments (veena, violin, tabla, mridangam) and became FRS (1924). Curious about the sea's blue colour, he found it was scattering of sunlight by water molecules and discovered the Raman Effect, proving light is made of photons, winning the 1930 Nobel Prize, the first Asian to do so. He used his mind as his laboratory and inspired students.
Discuss the contributions of Homi Bhabha and Vikram Sarabhai to Indian science.

Bhabha, after cosmic ray research at Cambridge, founded TIFR (1945), BARC and the Apsara reactor, was first chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission and the father of Indian nuclear science. Sarabhai studied cosmic rays under Raman, led the Aryabhata satellite effort, chaired INCOSPAR and AEC, set up TERLS, founded industries and the IIMs and saved crores by making antibiotics and military hardware in India.
